query: For the paper "Using Statistical and Semantic Models for Multi-Document Summarization" (arXiv: 1805.04579), answer this question: How exactly do they weigh between different statistical models?

drafts: Initially each model receives a uniform weight Wi = 1/g [5]. In the multi-document/domain-specific setting, weights Wi are fine-tuned on a training set of u domain-specific documents with gold-standard summaries, using the F1-score/F-measure as the factor [7], computed as Wi = (1/u)·Σ_{j=1}^{u} f(j,i), where f(j,i) is the F1 score of the ith model on the jth document [2]; a supervised learning algorithm captures mean model performances over the training data to fine-tune the summary [2]. These trained weights, together with the sense vector, are stored for future reference, and for single-document summarization the weights of the nearest stored vector are used [8]. The statistical models being weighted are TF/IDF, TextRank, and Jaccard/Cosine similarities [4].

The paper initially weights each model uniformly (Wi = 1/g), then fine-tunes the weights in the multi-document/domain-specific setting using F1 scores on domain-specific training documents with gold-standard summaries [5], [7].

Initially, before training, each of the g models is assigned the uniform weight Wi = 1/g, which is used in the cumulative sentence weight cWeight(si) = Σ_{j=1}^{g} Wi·B(j, si), where B(j, si) indicates whether sentence si appears in the summary of the jth model [5]. For multi-document/domain-specific summarization, they use a machine-learning approach: on a training set of u domain-specific documents with gold-standard/human-composed summaries, the weights Wi (i ∈ (1, g)) are fine-tuned taking the F1-score/F-measure as the factor [7]. The weight for each model is computed as Wi = (1/u)·Σ_{j=1}^{u} f(j,i), where f(j,i) denotes the F1 score for the jth model on the ith document; a supervised learning algorithm is used to capture the mean performances of different models over the training data to fine-tune the summary [2]. After training on the corpus, the weights are stored along with the sense vector for future reference, and for single-document summarization the weights of the nearest stored vector are used [8]. The statistical models being weighted are TF/IDF, TextRank, and Jaccard/Cosine similarities [4].

We hence used a su- pervised learning algorithm to capture the mean performances of different models over the training data to ﬁne-tune our summary.

Using weighing techniques in between various statistical models too further reﬁnes our result. For Statisti- cal models, we have used TF/IDF, Tex- tRAnk, Jaccard/Cosine Similarities. For Semantic Models, we have used WordNet- based Model and proposed two models based on Glove Vectors and Facebook’s InferSent. We tested our approach on DUC 2004 dataset, generating 100-word summaries. We have discussed the system, algorithms, analysis and also proposed and tested possible improvements.

3.6 Multi-Document/Domain-Speciﬁc Summarization We here use machine learning based approach to further increase the quality of our summa- rization technique. The elemental concept is that we use training set of u domain speciﬁc documents, with gold standard/human-composed summaries, provided we ﬁne tune our weights Wi∀i ∈(1, g) for different models taking F1- score/F-measure.(Powers, 2011) as factor.

For Multi-Document Summarization,after training on corpus, we assign weights among the different techniques .We store the sense vector for documents, along with weights, for future refer- ence. For Single document summarization, ﬁrstly we calculate the sense vector for that document and calculate the nearest vector from the stored Vectors, we use the weights of the nearest vector. We will describe the ﬂow for semantic and statis- tical models separately.
